The 2026 Farm Bill quietly slipped in three sections that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits, block states from regulating chemicals, and weaken water protections nationwide.

Rep. Chellie Pingree just introduced an amendment to delete them entirely.

Here’s the plain-English breakdown everyone should understand 👇

1. Lawsuit Shield for Pesticide Companies (Section 10205)

If this stays in the bill, chemical companies could avoid liability even if new evidence shows their product causes cancer or neurological damage. As long as the pesticide followed the label approved under Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), victims may lose the ability to sue.

Why this matters:

Bayer has already paid about $11 billion to settle lawsuits over the herbicide Glyphosate linked to non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. More than 165,000 claims have been filed against Bayer tied to the product Roundup herbicide.

If Section 10205 passes, future cases like those could be blocked.

Pingree’s amendment removes that shield.

2. States Lose Power Over Pesticide Rules (Section 10206)

Right now states and local governments can create stricter pesticide protections than the federal government.

That includes things like bans on spraying near schools or buffer zones around homes and waterways.

Section 10206 would override those rules nationwide.

That reverses precedent set by the Supreme Court case
Wisconsin Public Intervenor v. Mortier, which affirmed that local governments can regulate pesticides.

Seven states currently allow local pesticide control.
Those protections could disappear overnight.

3. Weakened Water & Wildlife Protections (Section 10207)

This provision would exempt pesticides from additional review under major environmental laws including the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act.

In practice that means pesticides approved by EPA could enter rivers, streams, and habitats without additional permits or environmental review.

Government monitoring has already detected pesticide residues in most U.S. waterways, raising concerns about runoff impacts on fish, wildlife, and drinking water.

Why This Fight Is Exploding

Critics argue the provisions protect chemical manufacturers, override state authority, and weaken environmental oversight.

Supporters claim the sections reduce litigation risk, simplify national pesticide regulation, and protect agricultural production.

Pingree’s amendment simply removes the three sections entirely, restoring the existing regulatory framework.

What Happens Next

The bill is still in markup inside the House Agriculture Committee.

That means these provisions can still be removed before the Farm Bill moves forward.

This fight will determine who controls pesticide rules in America — communities or chemical companies.

Key Takeaways

The Farm Bill includes three provisions that could shield pesticide companies from lawsuits.

They could also strip states and towns of authority to regulate pesticide use locally.

Environmental protections tied to waterways and wildlife could be weakened.

The Pingree amendment would remove those provisions entirely and restore current law. @amtoxicology @chelliepingree

S001198.text:
What a great day at the White House celebrating patriotism and football! First, President Trump presented the 2025 Commander in Chief's trophy to the U.S. Naval Academy football team for winning the famous annual Army-Navy football game and for beating the Air Force Academy Falcons. As a Marine and the Chairman of the Board of Visitors of the U.S. Naval Academy, I am always inspired when I get to meet these young men and women at our service academies on a regular basis—one of the best parts of serving on the Board.

The ceremony was particularly moving. Many of the Midshipmen standing behind the President at the event were First Classmen, on their way to be commissioned as officers in the Marine Corps and Navy in just a few months, serving their country during this dangerous time.

Then, the President signed an Executive Order, one that I have been pushing for a long time, to reserve most of the day on the second Saturday of December for “America’s Game”—the Army-Navy game—making sure that the growing number of college playoff and bowl games do not encroach on this scared annual Army-Navy game. This game brings Americans together, celebrates history, and reminds us of what matters most. It also showcases young Americans who’ve made the noble and courageous decision to serve our country, become leaders in our military, and, if called upon, lay down their lives for their fellow Americans. It’s such an important tradition that I led a letter in 2024 with dozens of members of the Senate and House, encouraging the leaders of the NCAA and College Football Playoffs to set aside time exclusively for the Army-Navy game. Now, thanks to the President’s Executive Order, that will happen. Go Navy!

There are few moments more meaningful for a community than the chance to thank someone who has spent a lifetime protecting it—and today, we had that chance with Middletown Township Police Department Officer Michael Marks.

For three decades, Mike has embodied the very best of public service — steady, selfless, and deeply committed to protecting our community. Whether serving in the K-9 Unit, as a Field Training Officer, department firearms instructor, or UAS pilot, he led with professionalism, strength, and integrity.

Each week, we share stories of those who leave a lasting mark on our community. This week, we honor a man whose life was defined not by what he sought, but by what he gave—freely, faithfully, and without pause: Levittown’s own Gerard “Jerry” Galloway, whom we sadly lost last week at 75 years old following a courageous battle with cancer.

Over the years, I had the privilege of getting to know Jerry through his deep involvement in our community. Spend even a few moments with him, and you quickly understood that his kindness was genuine, his faith was guiding, and his sense of purpose ran deep.

The eldest of ten children, Jerry carried with him the values instilled by his parents, Jim and Jane—a deep Catholic faith and a commitment to caring for others that would shape the course of his life.

In 1968, Jerry answered the call to serve our nation, drafted into the United States Army, where he served with honor and distinction. But for Jerry, service was never confined to a single chapter—it was the thread that ran through every part of his life. Following the Army, he pursued degrees in education and psychology, and dedicated his career to serving individuals with autism and intellectual disabilities.

His faith was not simply something he believed—it was something he lived. As a lifelong member of my home parish, Queen of the Universe, Jerry brought Holy Communion and companionship to those unable to attend Mass, ensuring no one felt forgotten.

Here in Bucks County, our annual St. Patrick’s Day Parade became a reflection of Jerry himself. Alongside his family, he helped build and sustain a tradition that brought people together in celebration of Irish heritage, faith, and community—something that meant so much to so many families, including my own. Year after year, Jerry carried that tradition forward with pride, warmth, and a deep sense of belonging that made everyone feel part of something bigger.

That was Jerry: steady in his faith, generous in his spirit, and grounded in a quiet strength that made people feel seen, valued, and at home.

Please join me in extending our deepest condolences to his beloved wife, Edna, his daughters, grandchildren, and all who knew and loved him.

For his faith, his service, and the countless lives he touched, Gerard “Jerry” Galloway will always be remembered as a true Hometown Hero.
